Dr. Newell W. Rossman^ Vice Chancellor of
Syracuse University, Greeted the 132nd
Convention at
Syracuse, New York. He
Expressed the Faith That Fraternities
Are a "Must''
The 132nd Convention of Psi Upsilon, held at the
Pi Chapter in Syracuse, New York, was honored by
the presence of Dr. Newell W. Rossman, Vice Chan
cellor of the University. To have been invited to open
the proceedings, he assured all present, was a distinct
privilege and pleasure. Portions of his exhilarating and
inspiring address to the assembled delegates will be
of interest to Diamond readers.
"It is always a
privilege to be introduced by old
friends, and Dr. John H. Hamel '36 is in that category.
I also want to pay tribute to all the Psi U's, both from
the Executive Council and locally, who have arranged
and masterminded this Convention.
"It is only fitting that a man like Bob Morey should
be your Fratemity President. I first worked with Bob
in 1950, when he was an oflBcer of the Morgan Guar
anty Bank and a Trustee of Syracuse University. Bob
is a man devoted to his family, to the banking pro
fession, to higher education, and to his fratemity.
"I am pleased to welcome the Psi Upsilon brother
hood to Syracuse University. If you will pardon the
cHche, some of my best friends are Psi U's. Indeed,
some of Syracuse University's best friends are Psi Vs.
And Syracuse University is proud to be a friend of
Psi Upsilon and of the Greek system.
"In discussing the Greeks at Syracuse University in
his two-volume work, the University's historian wrote:
All the Greek societies had been founded and their
existence permitted with the explicit approval of the
administration or with a tolerance that may astonish

It was a fitting and moving moment at the final
banquet when over two hundred members of Psi
Upsilon, both young and old, joined in the familiar
circle of clasped hands to close the proceedings of the
132nd Convention with the singing of "Dear Old
Shrine." This stirring expression of brotherhood con
stituted the last chapter of one of the finest Conven
tions that the Fraternity has held in recent years.
During the three days of the annual gathering,
seventy-two undergraduates were present from twentyfour of Psi Upsilon's twenty-six active Chapters, in
cluding twenty-six members of the Pi. Representing
fifteen Chapters were one hundred and fifty-seven
alumni in all, of whom one hundred and twenty-two
were members of the Pi, returning to honor the host
Chapter on the occasion of the One Hundredth Anni
versary of its founding. Executive Council members
among the alumni numbered seventeen. Special events
were graced by thirty wives, and Syracuse University
oflScials comprised the balance who were present for
portions of the celebration.
As President Robert W. Morey, Pi '20 had wished,
the Convention was comprehensive in scope, beauti
fully balanced between business sessions and com
mittee meetings, which were characterized by serious
discussion, and entertainment marked by good fellow
ship. The orchestration of this annual centering point
could best be described as always moving and yet un
hurried.
In the final session the business of the Convention
was completed, as resolutions aflFecting many areas of
the Fraternity's operation were presented. All bore
the earmark of considered judgment by the under
graduate delegates, directed to promoting the best in
terests and future of our Fraternit\'.
Chief among the decisions of the 132nd Convention
was the adoption of a reduced budget for 1975-76.
Coupled with plans for increasing the Fraternity's in
come, it was hoped that the 1974-75 deficit of nearh'
$25,000 could be pared to less than $7,000 in the year
ahead. At the same time preliminary steps were ap
proved for initiating a deferred giving program to in
sure the financial future of the Fraternity.
Other actions taken included the approval of a re
vised pledge manual in loose-leaf form, so that sup
plementary material can be added from time to time.
Fifteen hundred copies were prepared, so that each
pledge for the next several years may be given a copy.
A resolution was passed providing for the award of
certificates of merit to Psi Upsilon alumni upon the
presentation of nominations to succeeding Conven
tions by each Chapter and its alumni organization.
Finally, the functioning of the Executive Council was
strengthened by the establishment of a Steering Com
mittee, to be composed of five or seven members.
As the Convention schedule unfolded, it became in
creasingly clear that many members must have been
involved in the thoroughness of the planning. Accom
modations met every need, and meal arrangements
were timely and conveniently located. Special activi
ties were marked by their originality and by careful
provision for every contingency. Even the Convention
memento, a beautifully decorated plate, attested to no
detail having been left to chance. The packaging was
complete and coordinated.
One of the pleasant diversions was a visit to the
beautiful estate of Brother Edward C. Hughes, Pi '22.
He and his lovely wife were most gracious hosts, wel
coming each guest personally. The reception was held
on the sweeping lawn behind the Hughes home, with
a magnificent view afforded in all directions. A high
hght of the occasion was the happy participation of
the two young Hughes grandchildren, who first pro
vided expert parking directions and then circulated
among the visitors with an unending variety of cana
pes and cheeses.

Annual Communication of the Executive
Council to the 132nd Psi Upsilon Convention
For the loyalty and interest which each delegate
and guest has shown in expending time and funds to
attend this most important gathering of the Fratemity
the Executive Council is deeply grateful. We have
come together to accomplish the annual business of
Psi Upsilon and to celebrate with our brothers of the
Pi the One Hundredth Anniversary of the founding of
the sixteenth Chapter in our illustrious diadem. It has
had a
distinguished history in the century just com
pleted, and it is an outstanding Chapter today.
As we deliberate during the three days of this Con
vention, let us keep before us at all times the mission
of fraternity. It is pleasant living conditions, but it is
more. It is friendship and common interests, but a
good club can offer these, too. There remains an es
sential difference between a fraternity and a club. We
speak of bonds in a fraternity, and that is the keybonds of mutual obligation, bonds of caring, bonds
of responsibihty. We call a fellow member by the
name of brother, and we mean just that. When we re
peat the time-honored vows in the initiation cere
mony, we make a commitment�for life.
In that spirit we are pleased to present a brief re
port of our
stewardship as your Executive Council
for the past year. Four features perhaps are most
prominent:
1. Either your President or your Executive Vice
President, or both, visited every active Chapter of Psi
Upsilon between November and May. Other Council
members also have made visits where possible. Every
where we went, we received a warm and welcome
reception. Nearly every Chapter showed gains since
our last visit. In some cases it was a
sharply increased
pledge class, in others some
physical improvement, in
still others academic improvement or
progress else
where. The overriding characteristic that we found,
however, was a fift in spirit which was unmistakable
and exhilarating.
2. The Annual Giving program has taken another
forward leap of twenty-three per cent from $30,047
to $36,960. The increase may be attributed to the
leadership levels of giving superimposed upon the
regular membership levels, at which alumni who were
in a position to do so were invited to contribute.
3. Moving the office from Ann Arbor, Michigan to
Paoli, Pennsylvania, to accommodate the Executive
Vice President, and computerizing our extensive
alumni records have provided an
opportunity to estabhsh closer personal contacts with a wider number
and to lay the groimdwork for a modernized opera
tion.
4. With financial obstacles finally removed, the Psi
Upsilon Fellowship program was launched and the
first Psi Upsilon Fellow appointed. Louis S. Meny
hert of Jackson Heights, New York, the Delta Chap
ter's President this past year, joined the organization
on July first with an imposing Hst of credentials and
already has made an important contribution. With a
young alumnus in the Executive Office, a closer work
ing relationship between the Fratemity and the Chap
ter is high among our priorities for the coming year,
Offsetting these accompHshments, unfortunately,
are two areas of major concern:
1. The total collapse of the Nu Alpha Chapter at
Washington and Lee University in January closed a
sad struggle to rebound from a series of unanticipated
and mortal blows. At about the same time, the once
outstanding Theta Theta Chapter at the University
of Washington found its dwindhng membership re
duced to the very edge of survival. A spark of life
has been struck at the latter, it is encouraging to note,
and efforts will be made to revive the Nu Alpha,
2. Despite the increase in Annual Giving and pru
dent management of expenses, the Executive Council
incurred a deficit of nearly $25,000 in operations for
1974-75. Rehef from one-time expenses for moving
and computerization will be outweighed by the ex
pense of the Psi Upsilon Fellowship program, so that
a critical financial situation must be faced.
To these serious matters the 132nd Convention is
asked to give its closest attention. A host of related
subjects also will challenge the best thinking of the
able representatives who have come together in Syra
cuse on this occasion. As we reflect on this great mile
stone which the Pi Chapter today is passing, we think
of the rich and remarkable heritage which is oursone hundred and forty-two years of this unique entity

called Psi Upsilon. We are moved by the realization
of how our Fratemity has touched thousands upon
thousands of young men's lives in that span of time.
And we can face the future vdth faith and confidence,
I have always been proud of my long-standing mem
bership in Psi Upsilon. I have been proud, too, of my
membership in the Pi Chapter. And I came away from
the recent Convention hosted by the Pi in Syracuse

elated that there is that kind of spirit abroad among
our Chapters. It bodes well for the future of our Fra

Fifteen Grants to Undergraduates
For the 19754976 Academic Year
At the annual meeting of The Psi Upsilon Founda
tion, Inc. held at the University Club in New York
City on April 8, 1975, the Directors received the re
port of the Committee on Grants and approved its
recommendations for the coming year.
In addition to financial need, the Committee cited
other criteria weighed in the evaluation of appli
cants, such as integrity and strength of character,
sound academic standing, participation and leader
ship in campus activities, and willingness to accept re
sponsibility in Chapter affairs.
The Diamond is proud to present the following re
cipients :
Michael Balf,Xi'77
A native of Rockport, Massachusetts, Brother Balf
has demonstrated ability in all fields of endeavor. He
is described by both the University administration
and his Chapter Brothers as having "the initiative to
go beyond the perfunctory tasks assigned to him and
try to solve the problems that needed solving on his
own." A man of his convictions, an acceptor of re
sponsibility, and a doer by those who know him, he
has taken part in many diverse activities.
He was very active in student affahs and athletics
at Governor Dummer Academy and has followed
through with these interests at Wesleyan where he is
involved in sports, school government and student
pubhcations. Michael is on the varsity lacrosse team
and has shown what team spirit really means by giving
encouragement to all on the team and giving it his top
effort. His strong personal convictions are shown by
his commitment to the Middletown Farm Workers
Support Group and the Big Brother Movement. In
volved in the Big Brother organization since secondary
school. Brother Balf currently works with two chil
dren in Middletown, Connecticut.
In the Xi Chapter the same spii-it that he has shown
in community work and campus activities is also evi
dent. He was the Sophomore Vice President. Going
on to a position of greater responsibihty he became
tlie House Treasurer. An individual who expresses
himself more through his actions than his words, he
has won the respect and confidence of the Chapter.
On top of all this. Brother Balf is a scholar. He
has displayed a strong scholastic standing at the Uni
versity. The picture that emerges of Brother Michael
Balf is one of intellectual ability, integrity, and wit
that has won the friendship of his contemporaries as
well as the respect of his teachers. He is a young man
of considerable initiative, one who will most certainly
finish near the top of his class.
Gregory J. Brown, Epsilon Omega '77
When still a sophomore. Brother Gregory Brown
had served the Epsilon Omega Chapter as House
Manager, Steward and as an official delegate to
the 1974 Convention at the Iota Chapter. In all
these leadership positions he has consistently demon

William O. Davis, Delta '39, died May 10, 1974 in
the Veterans Administration Hospital in Washington,
D.C. after a long illness. He was 59 years old.
Dr. Davis, chief of the NOAA's upper atmosphere
and space services office, was general chairman last
year of the joint conference on the sensing of en
vironmental pollutants, a meeting sponsored by four
federal agencies and five professional societies.
A former Air Force colonel, he joined the Environ
mental Science Services Administiation in 1966, which
later was merged into the NOAA. Dr. Davis headed
the agency's plans and requirements division, the tele
communications and space services division and the
upper atmosphere and space services office.
He was a member of the team that planned and
coordinated the National Aeronautics and Space Ad
ministration's earth resources satellite program.
In the early 1950s, Dr. Davis was deputy command
er of the Air Force's Office of Scientffic Research;
then assistant director of laboratories at the Wright
Air Development Center in Ohio. In 1957, he headed
Project Farside, a program to obtain radiation and
magnetic data from space by launching a multistage
rocket from a high-altitude balloon.
In 1957, he organized the first symposium on astionautics held in the United States.
Dr. Davis leaves his wife, Virginia; two sons,
Charles T., and Michael W.; and two daughters, Mrs.
Kay Tohline and Melanie.
